newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Rescuers burrow into Peurto Rico blast site.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers burrow into Peurto Rico blast site.

text.p: Rescue teams finally began burrowing through rubble and debris on Saturday morning to the heart of a devastated San Juan commercial building where they expected to find a pile of corpses.
The unsafe condition of the six-storey shoe shop and office building had prevented searchers from entering deep inside the building since Thursday morning's blast, triggered by a suspected gas leak.
Nineteen people are confirmed dead but at least 11 more are missing. Rescuers do not expect to find any survivors.

Working overnight under arc lights, engineers managed to prop up a sagging central floor of the building and brace its teetering sides. Search and rescue teams, including crews from Miami and New York, began clearing a path through the debris on Saturday morning.
"The most important place is the basement," said Angel Martinez, rescue coordinator with the Puerto Rico Civil Defense. "I know we are going to find a lot of bodies there.
"The inside of the Humberto Vidal (building) was like a pile of pancakes," he said. "We've got the first, second and third floors in the basement. If we try to go too fast someone might get hurt."
Intermittent downpours have also held up the operation and made conditions more hazardous for search teams.
Martinez said it was unlikely they would find anyone alive, but "we never say no".
Rescuers feared they would find more bodies than the 11 listed as missing. "Those are employees reported by the supervisor. We don't know how many customers were inside," said Martinez.
The explosion occurred on Thursday morning just as the working day was beginning in Calle de Diego, a shopping street in San Juan's working class Rio Piedras district.
It gutted the Humberto Vidal building, severely damaged neighboring shops and showered a wide area with debris.

Authorities say the most likely cause was a gas leak although investigators, including agents from the FBI and National Transportation Safety Board, must also wait until the building is safe before they can begin their probe.
Governor Pedro Rossello said all the preliminary evidence pointed to a gas explosion but "obviously that is not a final conclusion."
"There is no indication it is anything else. The most prudent thing would be to let the investigation go on. It won't take that long," he added.
